evidence: src/infrastructure/http/createHttpApp.ts: createHttpApp(deps) builds the Express app, creates new OrderController(deps.orderUseCases) and new CatalogueController(deps.catalogueUseCases), and passes requireStaff(deps.staffApiKey) to createRouter
src/infrastructure/http/routes.ts: createRouter(controllers: Controllers, staffOnly: RequestHandler) is the single route table, and it applies staffOnly to every /staff/* route
src/infrastructure/http/routes.ts: all status transitions go through orders.changeStatus('pay'|'cancel'|'pack'|'ship'|'deliver'), so no transition rule is repeated
src/infrastructure/http/createHttpApp.ts: the /health route sits outside the router; this is a small placement choice, not a split of concern
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
Both files handle one concern: building the Express HTTP adapter. createHttpApp.ts sets up the app and its wiring: body parsing, the health check, building the controllers from the use cases, staff auth, and the not-found and error handlers. routes.ts holds the route table and takes the controllers and the staffOnly guard as parameters. The two files split the work cleanly, with no overlap.

The staff-access rule is defined once. createHttpApp.ts creates the guard by calling requireStaff(deps.staffApiKey). routes.ts applies the guard it is given to every /staff route.

Status changes always go through orders.changeStatus(action), so no transition logic is repeated. Cancel is exposed on both the customer path and the staff path, but both call the same controller method, so the rule still lives in one place.

The /health route is defined directly on the app in createHttpApp.ts rather than in routes.ts. This is a small placement choice and does not split the concern or bypass an abstraction. Neither file touches domain logic or controller internals directly.
